note: The household that carried the line down from Istria to the Kvarner coast, reconstructed from four register entries, the family's own MacFamilyTree file, eleven photographs the family holds, and the family's MyHeritage export of July 2018.

head.name: Josip Defranceschi

wife.name: Ana Kalanj
wife.born: 3 January 1864, at Rijenovica in the Vinodol
wife.note: Named as the mother in all four of their children's register entries; the 1905 burial entry writes her Ana Kalaj-Kučarica, adding the house-name. The 1896 death entry for their son Ivan calls her «Anica», the diminutive — the only place in the registers where she is named the way her household would have said it.

head.trade: vešti klesar sada tvorničar — a skilled stonemason, latterly a factory worker
head.tradeNote: The 1906 death entry gives Josip's occupation, and it settles the line's craft: «vešti klesar sada tvorničar» — a skilled stonemason, now a factory worker. His father Antonius was entered at Gračišće in 1863 as «lapicida», a stonecutter. Josip carried the trade down off the hill to the coast, and then the century took him out of it and into a factory.

children.name: Anton Rudolf
children.story: The line runs through him. Married Ursula Kovačina. On the Pfullingen list of foreigners in 1947 and certified by that town's mayor in 1950.

children.name: Marija Stjepanka
children.died: 29 September 1905, buried at Crikvenica the next day
children.story: Dead at twelve. The burial entry is the one that gives her mother's full style — Ana Kalaj-Kučarica.

children.name: Ivan
children.story: The name Ivan enters the family here — and goes out again eighteen months later. Entry 13 of the Crikvenica death register for 1896 records the death of Ivan De Franceschi, «Dvie /2/ godine», son of «Josip De Franceschi klesar i Anica rodjena Kalanj» — Josip Defranceschi, stonemason, and Anica née Kalanj. The cause is entered in one vernacular word, «Dobrac», which this archive has not been able to translate with confidence. No sacraments: he was two. He was buried on 28 March in the local parish cemetery by Carl Aleksander, the same priest who would bury his baby sister ten years later. Zorica was born on 14 December that year — conceived, by any ordinary reckoning, in the month her brother died.

children.name: Zorica
children.story: A Croatian name, and a plain one — the family had been on this coast six years.

children.name: Marija
children.died: 4 February 1906, aged three months and fifteen days
children.story: Dead of pneumonia — «upala pluća» — and buried on 6 February 1906 by Carl Aleksander, parish priest. Her elder sister Marija Stjepanka had died on 29 September 1905. This child was born about three weeks after that and given her name.

sons.name: Pepe
sons.story: Photographed in naval uniform with four other ratings, and again in shirtsleeves on a sea wall with the ZORA photographer's blindstamp in the corner. Married Božica Blašković, 1911–1994, also of Crikvenica; their son Toni lived 1937–1984. Pepe was born and died in the same town, and the archive had no dates for him at all until the family's MyHeritage file supplied both.

sons.name: Petar
sons.story: Ship's engineer with Jugoslav Lloyd at Split; left for Germany in April 1939; married Luise Salzer at Neuhausen in February 1942; applied in November 1947 to be resettled in California. The family's own caption on one photograph calls him a pilot in the war.

sons.name: Zdravko
sons.story: Taken by the Partisans in 1943 and held three or four months, then straight to Germany; motor mechanic at Reutlingen. Married Ruža Hreljac of Fužine. Resettled to Australia in 1949.

sons.name: Ivan
sons.story: Entered a Reutlingen factory on 21 October 1941, aged sixteen, as an unskilled hand. He went home. Married Hedviga Blažević of Senj, born 8 March 1926 — she died on 30 October 2001 at Johannesburg, six years to the day after him. He is buried on his own coast under a plain granite slab cut IVAN DEFRANČESKI.

nextGen.others: A sister, Anka, is named in the family's file with no dates. Felix, born 14 January 1908 at Crikvenica, stands on the Pfullingen list beside these men and appears in no register this archive has found and in no family file — he is either a late child of Josip and Ana, or an early one of Anton Rudolf. Poldo, or Pauldo, born 1901 at Crikvenica and dead in 1971, is photographed playing the accordion; the family's MyHeritage file places him instead among the nine children of the Imotski Franceschi, and which coast he belongs to is the one question at that seam still genuinely open.

australia.name: Ruža, born Hreljac
australia.story: Zdravko's wife. Buried at Horsham, South 2-D-23.

australia.name: Anton
australia.story: The child entered on the French camp card with the single word enfant across the fingerprint boxes. The family's MyHeritage file fixes the birth on the 22nd, settling a date the camp papers left as the 21st or 22nd. Married Marion Bain. Died 28 June 1999 and buried at Warrill Park, Willowbank, in the City of Ipswich, Queensland — and it is his death year, carried up a generation, that put 1999 on his father's entry in the family's file.

kovacina.heading: Ursula's people: the Kovačina of house 119
kovacina.lead: Anton Rudolf married Ursula Kovačina, and until now that was the whole of it — a surname with no family behind it. Two entries in the same Crikvenica death register give the household.

rows.what: Died at Crikvenica on 3 November 1904, aged 55, of pulmonary tuberculosis; sacraments administered; buried the next day by Carl Aleksander. The register gives his standing in full: «umirovljeni c. kr. financijski Nadstražar» — a retired Imperial-Royal financial senior guard, the Habsburg customs and excise service. He was born at Draga, in the kotar of Sušak, and lived at Crikvenica house 119.

His wife, entered as «kućarka» — housekeeper — and, by the time the clerk wrote the entry out, as «žena pokojnog Petra Kovačine Nadstražara», wife of the late Petar Kovačina. The name Uršula is standing in this family a generation before Anton Rudolf's wife carried it.

Entry 49 of 1898: dead at Crikvenica on 10 September, aged one year and six months, of «Tuberculosis pulmonum», buried on the 12th. Her parents are given as Petar Kovačina, son of Petar, «stolar» — a joiner — and Marija née Car, at house 119. The same house number as the financial guard, and the same first name; whether the joiner is the guard under an earlier trade, a brother, or a son, the register does not say and this archive will not guess.

kovacina.close: What can be said is that Crikvenica house 119 was a Kovačina house through the 1890s and 1900s, that consumption was in it twice, and that the name Ursula was already there. Ursula Kovačina, who married Anton Rudolf and bore Pepe, Petar, Zdravko, Ivan, Anka and Pero, is very likely a daughter or granddaughter of this household — but the marriage entry that would prove it has not been found, and the link is inference, not record.
kovacina.next: What to ask for: the Crikvenica marriage register for the 1900s and 1910s, for Anton Rudolf Defranceski and Ursula Kovačina; and the Crikvenica birth register around 1890 for a daughter of Petar Kovačina and Uršula Stojčić. Draga in the kotar of Sušak is a new place for this archive — nobody in the family has come from there before.

builtit.heading: One sentence in the family's own file about this house
builtit.quote: He built this house himself, for his family, but was lost due to family greed.
builtit.text: It is entered against Josip — «Josip Bepo de Franceschi» in the family's spelling — in the MacFamilyTree database the family has kept since at least 2021, and it is the only free-text note about him in the whole file. Everything else in the entry is a date or a place. This is somebody sitting down and typing what they had been told.
builtit.why: Two things follow. The first is that it agrees with the documents: the Crikvenica death register of 1906 calls him «vešti klesar sada tvorničar», a skilled stonemason now working in a factory, and his father at Gračišće was a lapicida. A stonecutter's son building his own house is exactly what the record says he was equipped to do. The second is that the house did not stay in the family, and the reason the family gives for it is a quarrel over the inheritance. This archive has no document for that and is not going to look for one; it is recorded here because it is the family's own account of how it lost the building this page is about.
builtit.source: «Defranceski Family Tree1», the family's MacFamilyTree database, last written 18 November 2021. The note is a user description attached to a fact record on Josip.

grave.heading: The family grave at Crikvenica, and what is left of it
grave.lead: This archive already holds a photograph of it standing. An upright stone with a cross and two oval porcelain medallions — a woman, and a man in a fedora — and cut across it: «Ovdje počiva u miru Božjem — ANA DE. FRANCESCHI — ✱ 19.IX.1863 ✝ 28.V.1936». Here rests in God's peace. It is on the gallery page of this site. It is also, it turns out, a photograph of something that is no longer there.
grave.now: The plot was visited again this year. What stands on it now is a black polished monument cut with OBITELJ JOVANOVIĆ, and a wide grey slab over the ground. Propped at the foot of it, resting on the edge of the slab beside a jar of flowers, is a small plaque of grey marble. It reads OBITELJ DEFRANCESKI — the Defranceski family — and carries three oval porcelain portraits: an older man in a suit and tie, the picture badly spotted; a young bearded man in a white polo-neck, smiling; and a woman in a dark jacket with a small cross at her throat. That plaque is the whole of what remains of the family's monument.
grave.account: The family's account of how that happened, recorded here as the family's own and not as a document: the plot was sold by a member of the family to the Jovanović family, and the Defranceski grave was taken apart. What is not in dispute, and is the reason this is on the page at all, is what is underneath. The family's dead were never moved. They are still in that ground.
grave.why: Two reasons to write it down rather than leave it. The first is evidentiary. Ana's stone is the single object at the centre of the oldest open question in this archive — whether Josip's wife was the Ana Kalanj of four Crikvenica baptismal entries or the Ana Grubišić, 19 September 1863 to 28 May 1936, whose name is cut on that stone. The stone is gone. The photograph of it is now the record, and this site holds it. The second is simpler. A family archive that only records what survives is a catalogue, not a memory. This one has already had to write down a house that Josip built and the family lost, and a chapel and a floor slab at Rijeka that may or may not still be standing. A grave taken apart belongs on the same page as the rest of it.
grave.source: Photographed by the family at the Crikvenica cemetery, 2026. The earlier photograph of the intact stone is plate «ana-grave» in this archive's gallery, from the family's own files. The account of the sale is the family's.

kalanj.heading: The Kalanj of Klenovica
kalanj.lead: The oldest open question on this archive's log is whose daughter Josip married. Four Crikvenica baptismal entries name Ana Kalanj, and her own baptism survives at Ledenice — 3 January 1864, daughter of Josip Kalanj and Rosalia née Perković, at Rijenovica house 22 in the Vinodol. Against that, the family holds a photograph of a gravestone for an Ana Grubišić. The family has now walked the cemetery at Klenovica, and it is full of Kalanj.
stones: Ten on one monument, over three generations, with porcelain portraits for every one of them. The oldest, Marija, born five years after the archive's Ana Kalanj.
An Ana Kalanj, 1899–1996 — a different woman, born thirty-five years after ours, and a reminder that the given name runs in the family too.
Mate 1909–1997, with a slab beside him: Kata 1861–1943, Luka 1893–1944, Ivan 1895–1955, Marija 1901–1985
Kata, born 1861, is the closest in age to the archive's Ana — three years apart.
Worn and read at an angle; the dates for the second and third are not legible here.
kalanj.why: None of these is Ana. The earliest of them, Kata born 1861, is three years older than the Ana Kalanj the registers give Josip, and every other stone is later. What the cemetery does establish is the thing the argument actually needs: the Kalanj are not an incidental name in a register. They are one of the standing families of this stretch of coast, buried ten to a monument at Klenovica — the village where this archive's generation 5 lived at house 22. A Gračišće stonecutter's son who came down to the Kvarner and married a Kalanj married into the place, and the place is still full of them.
kalanj.next: And it sharpens what to ask for. The Klenovica and Ledenice parish books will hold the Kalanj as a connected series, not as isolated entries. Ana's parents — Josip Kalanj and Rosalia Perković of Rijenovica house 22 — should be findable in them, and so should her marriage.
kalanj.source_kalanj: Photographed by the family at the Klenovica cemetery, 2026. Fourteen monuments carrying the name were recorded; the transcriptions above are from those photographs, and where a stone is worn or read at an angle that is said.

whotaken.heading: Which of them the Partisans took, and what the papers actually say
whotaken.lead: The family remembers that it was Anton — Anton Rudolf Defranceski, born 1890, the father — who was taken by the Partisans. The documents this archive holds put it on his son. Both things happened in the same year, in the same household, and it is not hard to see how the two became one memory. Here is what each record says.

rows.text: Anton Rudolf Defranceski, born 20 January 1890 at Klenovica house 22 and baptised on 9 February, married Ursula Kovačina, and their children were Josip «Pepe» (1911), Petar (1913), Zdravko (1921), Ivan (1925) and Anka. He is the father of the three brothers, exactly as remembered.

rows.lab: But the seizure is recorded of Zdravko
rows.text: It comes from Zdravko's own resettlement file — what he told the International Refugee Organisation when they registered him after the war, under IRO number 148.901. Taken by the Partisans in 1943, held three or four months, then sent to Germany, where he worked as a motor mechanic at Reutlingen. It is a first-person account given by the man it happened to, into an official record, within a few years of the event. That is about as good as this kind of evidence gets.

rows.lab: And Anton was not in Germany when it happened
rows.text: The Pfullingen and Reutlingen papers show Anton at Pfullingen for three and a half months only — 1 March to 13 June 1942 — and then he went home. This site already says the consequence out loud: if the family is right that he died in 1943, he died back on the Kvarner and not in Germany. So father and son were in the same country in 1943, and one of them was taken and the other died.

rows.lab: Which is very likely why the memories merged
rows.text: Two catastrophes in one house in one year: the father dead, the twenty-two-year-old son seized and carried off to Germany. Eighty years on, in a family that ended up scattered across three continents, those two things collapsing into one sentence is the most ordinary thing in the world. The archive's job is not to correct the memory out of existence but to say which part of it each document supports.

whotaken.open: And it leaves a real question, which is worth asking plainly: how did Anton Rudolf die in 1943? This archive has never had a date, a place or a cause for it — the year comes from the family, not from a document, and it is the only fact about him on this site that does. He came home from Germany in June 1942. In 1943 the Kvarner was under German occupation after the Italian collapse in September, with Partisan units in the hills behind Crikvenica. His son was seized that year. If the family memory attaches the Partisans to Anton rather than to Zdravko, that may be a confusion of two events — or it may be that both are true and the archive has only ever documented one of them. The Crikvenica death register for 1943 would settle it in an afternoon, and it is now the first thing on the list.
whotaken.source_taken: Zdravko's IRO resettlement record, number 148.901, and Petar's, 148.902; the Pfullingen register of foreigners of 1947 and the town's certifications of 1950; the Klenovica baptismal register for 20 January 1890. Anton Rudolf's death in 1943 is family testimony and is published as such.
